newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa still hopes for Zaire talks before Monday.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa still hopes for Zaire talks before Monday.

text.p: South Africa said on Wednesday it still hoped to get Zaire's warring leaders together on a navy ship for peace talks by the weekend despite President Mobutu Sese Seko's reluctance.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Tuesday both he and the ailing Mobutu had agreed to meet on the South African supply ship in the Atlantic off the West coast of Zaire, but a U.S. source later said Mobutu had turned down the offer.

South African deputy foreign minister Aziz Pahad told state radio he had been surprised by the setback as both men had agreed to talks on the SAS Outeniqua, which is waiting off Zaire, but still hoped to get them to meet for the first time before Monday.
"We were hoping the meeting would take place before the weekend, but now we are still confident it will take place before the weekend is over," he said.
President Nelson Mandela was due to chair the talks but might not be able to if there are long delays, officials said.
Kabila, in control of all major cities bar the capital, appealed to the international community to force Mobutu to attend the talks at sea to avoid a battle for Kinshasa.
He told Reuters he would not go to nearby Gabon, a venue preferred by Mobutu and encouraged by the United States, for security reasons.
"Only talks will avoid a battle for Kinshasa. But if Mobutu cannot come to talks then it is business as usual for us. It means we will have to take Kinshasa," he said.
Despite the U.S. diplomat's downbeat remarks on Tuesday, Mobutu's son and spokesman Nzanga Mobutu declined on Wednesday to rule out talks off the coast of Zaire.
Pahad said the naval vessel had been chosen as a compromise venue close to Zaire where both Mobutu and Kabila, suspicious of each other, could be assured of their safety.
"This venue was agreed to after long attempts to find a suitable venue acceptable to both. Kabila has publicly said this is the venue he now accepts and he won't consider another," he said.
Pahad, warning that time was running out, said U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was in the region to iron out any late security or logistical concerns.
U.N. sources said Sahnoun went first to the Angolan capital Luanda to see President Eduardo dos Santos.
Kabila's forces have been battling since October to oust the cancer-stricken Mobutu and have captured more than half the vast central African country, much of it without a fight.
They are now closing in on Kinshasa, a sprawling city of several million which diplomats fear could see a bloody battle, widespread looting and mayhem if Kabila tries to take it by force.
